newsitem.title: KENYA: U.S. attacks U.N. environment agency, China differs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. attacks U.N. environment agency, China differs.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday led calls for reform and budget cuts in the U.N. environment agency, calling it "disjointed and in a state of crisis" but China threw her weight behind the developing world's clamour for more aid.

William Dilday, head of the U.S. delegation at the governing council of the U.N. Environment Programme, UNEP's top legislative and policy organ, told delegates from 100 nations and agencies the organisation needed surgery not more funds.
"We believe strongly that UNEP is a very important agency, unfortunately we find this agency with a set of problems. It is in a state of crisis," Dilday told a hushed audience.

He added: "We have seen a significant deterioration of political capabilities and programmes of UNEP. We need to streamline UNEP so it can work better. It is currently simply too disjointed to administer."

Dilday spoke after the developing world backed by a powerful Chinese vote urged the rich West to raise funding for UNEP so it can effectively concentrate on managing and using natural resources, building a better environment for human health.

But taking a hardline stand, Dilday rejected Third World demands saying "We need to transform UNEP and stop its fragmentation. But throwing more money at UNEP's problems is not an answer to the problems."
Dilday said UNEP's governing structure, its programmes and administration were in need of "comprehensive reform."

"Better governance, consistent or transparent governance will help UNEP. The system we have here (at UNEP) is simply not working," Dilday said, adding that the U.S.'s sharp criticism was driven by commitment to the global environment.
Western governments are critical of the U.N. agency, saying it appeared less effective since the 1992 Earth summit in Brazil.
The Earth summit, the U.N. Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED), gathered world leaders in Rio de Janiero, where they made fresh commitments to environmental protection.
Western governments led by the United States want UNEP, the only global U.N. agency based in the developing world, to refocus on its core tasks.
These are identified as monitoring the state of the planet, identifying emerging issues and initiating global responses to them and promoting the development of international law.
The United States has spearheaded calls for steep cuts in the UNEP budget as part of its attack on U.N. agencies it considers wasteful, inefficient or outdated.
The governing council meets every two years at UNEP's Nairobi headquarters and is normally used to approve a programme on managing natural resources and improving the environment.
But this year's forum is being sidetracked by talk of reforms and finance because of failure by the West to pay dues.
China on Tuesday endorsed a position adopted by the Group of 77 calling for raised aid and for implementation of mainly Third World UNEP programmes abandoned last year for lack of funding.

"The Group of 77 and China cannot support the revision of the programme of work because it has deleted many of the projects which the members of this group are concerned about," said a joint statement issued by China and the Group.
Nigeria, speaking on behalf of the Group of 77 and China, attacked the western position terming it "lack of will."
"What is lacking is the will by the rich countries to help developing nations manage their environment," said Clarkson Umelo, Nigerian ambassador and permanent representative to UNEP.
UNEP has seen its budget drop sharply over the last few years as donors link more funding to reforms in the agency.
From a budget of $160 million during UNEP's 1991-92 programme, UNEP's budget fell to $105 million in the last two years and even then only $62.5 million was disbursed by donors.
New U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has promised to reform the entire U.N. system and has made reform a constant theme since his election last December.
Washington vetoed his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, charging him with failure to press reform of the 185-nation organisation with sufficient vigour.
